kapak.alt: An older adult, from needs to follow-up

youtube.baslik: Case: An Older Adult's First Hearing Aid Journey | Lesson 279 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional case, we follow an older adult who will use a hearing aid for the first time: needs assessment, concrete goals with the COSI, barriers and supports, device selection, verification with NAL-NL2 and real-ear measurement, the first fitting day, acclimatization, data logging and follow-up appointments.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Dillon et al., Client Oriented Scale of Improvement (1997); Keidser et al., The NAL-NL2 prescription procedure (2011); ASHA, Hearing Aids for Adults; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: An older adult, from needs to follow-up
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we follow, from start to finish, an older adult who will use a hearing aid for the first time.
We will cover needs assessment and personal goals, verification with NAL-NL2 and real-ear measurement, acclimatization and follow-up visits.

maddeler.metin: TV volume is _a source of arguments_

cumleler: Our case is fictional: a seventy-two-year-old woman comes in for a hearing aid assessment.
She came with her husband, who says that in recent years she gives wrong answers to questions and often asks for repeats.
Because she turns the TV up very loud, there are sometimes arguments at home.
She struggles most at family dinners; when several people talk at once, she loses the conversation and falls silent.
She has trouble understanding her grandchildren's high voices, and this upsets her.
She is willing to try hearing aids, but she has concerns about appearance, learning to use them, and cost.
Otoscopy and tympanograms are normal in both ears; the audiogram shows a loss sloping toward the high frequencies in both ears.
Bone conduction overlaps air conduction; the loss is sensorineural, with no significant asymmetry between the ears.
The pure-tone average is about forty decibels in both ears; the loss is mild in the lows and moderate to severe in the highs.
Word recognition scores are eighty-four percent on the right and eighty percent on the left; consistent with the loss.
This picture may fit age-related hearing loss; an ENT exam was also done, and no barrier to hearing aids was reported.
The loss at the frequencies that carry high consonants fits her difficulty in crowds and with high voices.
With the Client Oriented Scale of Improvement, or COSI, we set the person's own goals.
The person chooses up to five specific situations to improve; the first goal is joining the conversation at Sunday family dinners.
The second goal is watching TV at a volume that does not disturb her husband.
The third goal is having weekly phone calls with her daughter without strain.
The fourth goal is understanding her grandchildren's questions the first time.
Goals are written as concretely as possible and ranked by importance; each will be assessed separately at follow-up.
Vision problems can make small parts and buttons hard to see; in our case, she uses reading glasses.
She says that, because of stiff finger joints, she may struggle to change small batteries.
We talk about expectations: hearing aids will help in noise too, but they will not bring hearing back to normal.
Her concerns are taken seriously; the look and use of the devices are explored together with sample devices.
Her husband's willingness is a great support; he is encouraged to attend the fitting and follow-up visits.
Because the loss is symmetric in both ears, bilateral hearing aids are recommended.
Listening with two ears helps with understanding in noise and finding where sound comes from.
Selection weighs the loss, the ear canal, dexterity, vision and the person's preferences together.
With a mild low-frequency loss, a behind-the-ear device with the receiver in the canal and an open fit may be a suitable option.
Because her dexterity is limited, a rechargeable model removes the trouble of changing batteries.
For the TV goal, wireless streaming or a TV accessory is discussed.
Options are explained with their benefits and limits; the decision is made together with her and her husband.
The device is set to her audiogram with NAL-NL2, the prescription formula of Australia's National Acoustic Laboratories.
But the software estimate does not fully show the sound produced in her own ear canal.
So a thin probe tube is placed in the ear canal, near the tympanic membrane, and measurements are made with the device in place.
With a speech-like signal from a loudspeaker, the sound level in the ear canal is measured and compared with the target.
Real-ear measurement shows whether the device reaches the prescription target; this is called verification.

bolgeler.etiket: up to 2 kHz: plus or minus 5 dB

notlar.metin: Write the reason in the file

cumleler: In the chart, the navy dashed line shows a sample prescription target for average speech.
The red line is the measurement with the manufacturer's first fit; it is clearly below target, especially from two thousand hertz up.
Research shows that manufacturers' first-fit settings often fall below the prescription target.
The measurement after adjustment, the green line, is within five decibels of the target up to two thousand hertz.
A common approach is for the measurement to be within plus or minus five decibels of target, especially up to two thousand hertz.
For this first-time user, gain left a little below target in the high frequencies will be raised step by step as she acclimatizes.
Every measurement, and the reason for any deliberate departure from target, is written in the file.
The first fitting day starts with physical fit: is the device comfortable, is there pressure in the canal, is there feedback?
Then fit to target is verified with the real-ear measurement we have just seen.
She inserts and removes the devices several times with her own hands, while her husband watches.
Care steps such as charging, cleaning and changing domes are explained as a simple routine and given in writing.
Phone calls and the TV connection are tried in the clinic, so the first try at home does not end in disappointment.
Understanding of key information is checked by having her repeat it in her own words.

maddeler.metin: New sounds may seem _loud and artificial_
Her own voice may sound different
Gain is raised step by step

cumleler: The brain readjusting to sounds it has not heard for years is called acclimatization.
In the first days, rustling paper, running water and footsteps may seem unusually loud and artificial; this is expected.
The most effective way to acclimatize is to wear the devices regularly all day, not only in difficult places.
Starting at home and in quiet places in the first days, then moving to crowded places, puts the person at ease.
Her own voice sounding different is also a common complaint, and it often fades with time or is fixed by adjustment.
At follow-up visits, gain is raised step by step toward target, as comfort allows.

maddeler.metin: Choose a quiet corner in noise

cumleler: Hearing aids alone are not enough; we teach her and her husband some strategies: get her attention by name before speaking.
Speak face to face, where she can see your face, instead of calling from another room.
When a sentence is not understood, say it again in other words instead of shouting the same sentence.
Turn down the TV or radio while talking.
At family dinners, sitting where she can see everyone, away from noise sources, also helps the first goal.

sahneler.metin: On the first day, do not end the visit until the person has inserted and removed the device several times by hand; include the spouse too.
cumleler: A tip from the field: on the fitting day, do not end the visit until the person has inserted and removed the device several times herself.
A device she cannot put in cannot be used at home; this is one of the common reasons for giving up in the first weeks.
When a spouse or caregiver also sees these steps, small problems can be solved at home.
A short phone call in the first days after fitting catches small problems before they grow.
In the first days after fitting, a short phone call asks how use is going.
The check in the first weeks covers comfort, sound quality and problems with use; fine-tuning is done if needed.
The device's data logging objectively shows daily hours of use and the settings it was used in.
A few months later, outcomes are assessed with the COSI goals and standard questionnaires.
The timing of follow-up appointments is planned by the clinic's protocol and the person's needs.
After that, audiogram and device checks continue at regular intervals.
This chart shows the average daily hours of use in our case over the first four weeks.
In the first week the devices were used for an average of three and a half hours a day, mostly only while watching TV in the evening.
In the phone call, the importance of all-day use was explained again.
By the fourth week, daily use rises to eight and a half hours.
Short hours of use may signal discomfort, expectations or a physical problem; the reason is always asked.
The log is not a policing tool but the starting point for solving problems together with the person.
At three months, she rates joining the conversation at family dinners as much better.
The TV is now at a level that does not disturb her husband; this goal is also much better.
Change on the phone has been limited; the phone listening setting and wireless connection will be worked on again.
There is also a clear improvement in understanding her grandchildren's questions.
Looking goal by goal clearly shows what works and which areas still need work.

cumleler.yazi: Overall satisfaction is also measured with a short questionnaire such as the International Outcome Inventory for Hearing Aids, or IOI-HA.
cumleler.ses: Overall satisfaction is also measured with a short questionnaire such as the International Outcome Inventory for Hearing Aids, or I O I H A.

maddeler.metin: Needs assessment and concrete COSI goals
NAL-NL2 target, verified by real-ear measurement

cumleler: The first hearing aid process starts with a needs assessment involving the person and family, and concrete COSI goals.
The device is set with a prescription formula, and its fit to target is verified by real-ear measurement.
For acclimatization, regular all-day use is advised; gain is brought toward target step by step if needed.
Planned follow-up visits, data logging and outcome assessment with the COSI complete the process.

sahneler.soru: The manufacturer's first fit is below target. What next?
secenekler: Bring it to target with REM
sahneler.aciklama: Real-ear measurement verifies _fit to target_; for a first-time user, gain can be raised step by step.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: on real-ear measurement, the manufacturer's first fit is clearly below target in the highs. What should be done?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the fitting is brought toward target, guided by real-ear measurement.
For a first-time user, gain may be kept slightly low for comfort at first; but the plan is to reach target step by step.
